title: Rules, Hands and Betting
intro: This page covers what a beginner needs: how a hand of Texas hold'em is played, how hands rank, how the betting works and what the positions at the table are called. Hold'em is the most played form of poker, so the rest of the topic uses it, but most of the ideas carry over to the other forms listed at the end.

blocks.text: Each player is dealt two cards face down, their hole cards. Five shared community cards are then dealt face up in the middle of the table, in three stages, with a round of betting before the first stage and after each one. Each player makes the best five-card hand they can from their two hole cards and the five community cards, using both, one or neither of their own cards.

items: Blinds. Before the cards are dealt, the two players to the left of the dealer put in forced bets: the small blind (SB, usually half a big blind) and the big blind (BB). Without them nobody would have a reason to bet. Some games also take an ante, a small forced bet, from every player (or, in many tournaments, one big-blind ante paid by the big blind for the whole table).
Preflop. Each player gets two hole cards. Betting starts with the player to the left of the big blind and goes clockwise.
Flop. Three community cards are dealt at once, then a betting round. From here on the first active player to the left of the dealer acts first.
Turn. A fourth community card, then a betting round.
River. The fifth and last community card, then the last betting round.

Showdown. If two or more players remain after the river betting, they show their hands and the best five-card hand wins the pot. Hands that are exactly equal split it (a split pot or chop). If every other player folds at any point, the last player wins the pot without showing.

blocks.text: A dealer button marks the player who is the nominal dealer for the hand; it moves one seat clockwise after each hand, so every player takes their turn at each position and pays the blinds equally often.

items: Check: bet nothing and pass the action on. Only possible when nobody has bet yet on this round.
Bet: put chips in when nobody has yet on this round. The first bet on the preflop round is the big blind itself.
Call: match the current bet.

Raise: increase the current bet. Others must then call the larger amount, raise again or fold. The first raise preflop is called an open (an open-raise); a re-raise is a 3-bet (the blind counts as the first bet), the next one a 4-bet, and so on.
Fold: give up the hand and any chips already put in.

All-in: put in all of your chips. A player all-in for less than the bet can only win, from each other player, as much as they put in; the extra chips go to a side pot contested by the players who covered them.

blocks.text: A betting round ends when every player still in the hand has put in the same amount (or is all-in) and everyone has had a chance to act. Limping is entering the pot preflop by just calling the big blind instead of raising; in modern no-limit play it is mostly a sign of a weak player, except from the small blind.

items: No-limit (NL): a player may bet any amount up to all of their chips at any time. The minimum bet is the big blind, and a raise must be at least as large as the last bet or raise. No-limit hold'em (NLHE) is the most popular game in the world.
Pot-limit (PL): the largest bet or raise is the size of the pot, counting the call. Omaha is usually played pot-limit (PLO).

Fixed limit (FL or limit): bets and raises come in fixed sizes, a small bet on the first two rounds and a big bet (twice as large) on the turn and river, usually capped at four bets per round. With every bet the same size, limit poker is much more about pot odds and much less about bet sizing.

blocks.text: The stack is the chips a player has in front of them, usually measured in big blinds. A cash game (ring game) uses real money chips, and players can join, leave or buy more chips any time; most games start everyone with 100 big blinds. A tournament gives everyone the same starting chips, blinds rise on a schedule and players are knocked out until one has every chip; prizes go to the last few. Tournaments change the mathematics, see #/poker/tournaments.

From strongest to weakest. The counts are the number of distinct five-card hands of each kind from a 52-card deck, out of $\binom{52}{5} = 2{,}598{,}960$; the rarer a kind, the higher it ranks. The last column is how often a hold'em player's best five of seven cards (two hole cards and five on the board) is that kind, if they stay to the river.

items: Ties are broken by rank: a pair of kings beats a pair of queens; between two equal pairs the highest unpaired cards decide. These deciding side cards are the kickers: AK beats AQ on a board of A 9 7 4 2 because the king kicker beats the queen.
A full house ranks first by its three of a kind, then by its pair. Two flushes compare their highest cards, then the next, and so on.
Suits never rank: two hands that differ only in suit split the pot.
The ace plays high or low in a straight: A K Q J T is the highest straight (Broadway) and 5 4 3 2 A the lowest (the wheel). A straight cannot wrap round: Q K A 2 3 is not a straight.

Flushes, straights and full houses beat three of a kind even though, in the best five of seven cards, three of a kind is not much more common. The order comes from the five-card counts, not the seven-card ones.

blocks.alt: An oval table with nine seats. Going clockwise from the bottom: BTN (the dealer button, marked D), SB, BB, UTG, UTG+1, MP, LJ, HJ and CO. Each seat has a number for its order of action before the flop: UTG 1 through CO 6, BTN 7, SB 8 and BB 9. Early seats are blue, middle purple, late green and the blinds grey.
blocks.caption: The positions at a full table. At a six-handed table the first three seats after the big blind are dropped, and the first to act is often called UTG or LJ.

items: Early position: under the gun (UTG, the first to act preflop) and the seats just after it. They act first and have the most players still to act behind them, so they play the fewest hands.
Middle position: the middle seats (MP), up to the lojack (LJ) and hijack (HJ).
Late position: the cutoff (CO) and the button (BTN). The button acts last on every round after the flop, the best seat at the table.

The blinds: the small and big blind act last before the flop but first after it, and have already put money in. They lose money in the long run even for the best players; the aim in the blinds is to lose as little as possible.

blocks.text: Being in position (IP) on a player means acting after them on the flop, turn and river; being out of position (OOP) means acting first. Why position is worth so much is covered on #/poker/strategy.

items: Omaha (PLO): four hole cards instead of two, and a hand must use exactly two of them with exactly three from the board. With six two-card combinations in every hand, hands run much closer in equity and big hands are much more common. Five- and six-card versions also exist.
Seven-card stud: no community cards. Each player gets seven cards of their own, some face up, over five betting rounds, and makes their best five.
Draw poker: five hidden cards, with one or more chances to swap some for new ones. Five-card draw is the classic home game.

Lowball: the lowest hand wins. In ace-to-five lowball (as in Razz, a stud game) straights and flushes don't count and 5 4 3 2 A is the best hand; in deuce-to-seven lowball (as in 2-7 triple draw) aces are high, straights and flushes count against you, and 7 5 4 3 2 of mixed suits is the best.

High-low split (hi-lo, such as Omaha hi-lo or stud eight-or-better): the pot is split between the best high hand and the best qualifying low hand, which must have five different cards of eight or lower. Winning both halves is scooping.
Short-deck (six-plus) hold'em: the 2s to 5s are removed, leaving 36 cards. Flushes become rarer than full houses and rank above them, and the ace can make A 6 7 8 9 as the lowest straight.
Mixed games, such as HORSE (hold'em, Omaha hi-lo, Razz, stud, stud eight-or-better), rotate through several forms.

blocks.title: Reading a showdown
blocks.text: The board is Kh Qh 7c 7d 2h. Player A holds Ah 3c, player B holds Ks Kc, player C holds Qs 7s. Who wins?
blocks.hint: Find each player's best five cards from their two and the board's five, then compare the kinds of hand first.
solution: A uses Ah with the board's Kh, Qh and 2h but needs a fifth heart: there are only four hearts in total (Ah, Kh, Qh, 2h), so no flush. A's best hand is a pair of sevens with A K Q kickers.
B has kings full of sevens: Ks Kc Kh 7c 7d, a full house.
C has sevens full of queens: 7s 7c 7d Qs Qh, also a full house. Full houses compare their three of a kind first, so kings full beats sevens full.
blocks.answer: B wins with a full house, kings full of sevens

blocks.title: Side pots
blocks.text: Three players go all-in before the flop: A with 20 bb, B with 50 bb and C with 100 bb. C covers both. How are the pots made up, and what does each player put in?
blocks.hint: Each player can win from every other player only as much as they put in themselves.
solution: Main pot: 20 bb from each of the three, 60 bb in all. All three can win it.
First side pot: another 30 bb from each of B and C (50 - 20), 60 bb in all. Only B and C can win it.
C's other 50 bb are not called by anyone and go back to C. If A has the best hand, B the second best and C the worst, A wins the 60 bb main pot and B wins the 60 bb side pot.
blocks.answer: a 60 bb main pot for all three and a 60 bb side pot for B and C; C gets 50 bb back
